chapters.title: Oscar Wilde and His Only Novel
paragraphs: The Picture of Dorian Gray is the only novel written by Oscar Wilde, and it may be the most beautiful and the most dangerous book of the eighteen-nineties. Wilde was born in Dublin in 1854, the son of a famous surgeon and a celebrated poetess, and he became the most brilliant conversationalist in London: a dandy in velvet and lilies who turned the dinner table into a stage and the epigram into an art form. At Oxford he absorbed the doctrine of art for art's sake, and he spent the rest of his life preaching it — beauty needs no excuse, no moral, no apology.

The novel first appeared in June 1890 in an American magazine, Lippincott's Monthly Magazine. It caused an immediate scandal. Reviewers called it unclean, effeminate, and poisonous; one newspaper demanded that the authorities prosecute it. Wilde answered his critics with wit and fury, and the following year he published a longer, revised version in book form — twenty chapters instead of thirteen — with a new Preface made entirely of glittering aphorisms, each one a small bomb aimed at Victorian respectability.

That Preface is the manifesto of aestheticism, the movement Wilde embodied. There he wrote some of the most famous lines in all of literature, and they deserve to be quoted exactly: "There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written, or badly written. That is all." And again: "The only excuse for making a useless thing is that one admires it intensely." The word "useless" is a provocation: Wilde meant that art must not be useful, must not preach, must not improve the reader. Art exists for beauty alone.

The same Preface gives us another line that readers have carried with them for more than a century: "All art is at once surface and symbol." Wilde wanted his readers to go beneath the surface — but he warned them, in the same breath, that anyone who tries to read a moral lesson into a work of art will find only their own corruption reflected back. It is a magnificent paradox, and it has haunted the novel ever since, because the story itself seems to preach the most terrible moral of all.

The paradox deepened five years later. In 1895 Wilde was put on trial for "gross indecency," prosecuted after his disastrous libel suit against the Marquess of Queensberry. In the courtroom, the prosecution read passages from Dorian Gray aloud and called it a poisonous book that had corrupted young men. Wilde defended himself brilliantly, but he was convicted and sentenced to two years of hard labor in Reading Gaol. The novel that had proclaimed art's innocence became, in the public mind, evidence of its author's guilt.

Wilde always insisted the book had no moral purpose. In letters he wrote that the novel's real moral was simply this: all excess, as well as all renunciation, brings its own punishment. He compared his three main characters to aspects of himself: Basil Hallward was what he thought he was, Lord Henry was what the world thought he was, and Dorian was what he would like to be — in other ages, perhaps. The comparison is a confession and a warning at once.

The longer 1891 edition is the version most readers know today. Wilde added six chapters, softened a few passages that had caused the greatest outrage, and — most importantly — added the Preface, turning his defense into part of the work itself. He also deepened the character of James Vane and expanded Dorian's years of corruption into the great eleventh chapter, that perfumed catalogue of the senses. The book as we have it is therefore a palimpsest: a magazine story, a scandal, a revised novel, and a manifesto, all in one.

Why does this novel still matter? Because it asks, more elegantly than any other book, the question every age must answer: what happens when a human being decides that beauty is the only god worth worshipping? Wilde gives us a young man of extraordinary loveliness who trades his soul for eternal youth, and then follows him, chapter by chapter, into the cold country where that bargain leads. The prose is perfumed and musical; the conversations sparkle like champagne; and underneath the sparkle runs a current of genuine horror.

In prison Wilde wrote De Profundis, the long letter that is his spiritual autobiography, and after his release he lived in exile in France under an assumed name. He never recovered his position, and he never wrote another novel — as if Dorian Gray had said everything he had to say in that form, and said it at too high a price. The book survived its author, outlived the scandal, and entered the canon: the wittiest horror story in English, and the most haunting defense of beauty ever written.

This selection gathers the novel's essential scenes in order: the painter's studio where the fatal portrait is finished, the seductive philosophy that poisons Dorian's mind, the love of the actress Sibyl Vane and its cruel destruction, the slow corruption of eighteen years, a murder, a haunting, one last attempt at goodness, and the unforgettable ending. Between the famous passages you will find faithful narration of the connecting story, so the whole arc of Wilde's fable can be read as one continuous tale.

chapters.title: Basil Hallward's Studio
paragraphs: The novel opens in the studio of the painter Basil Hallward, on a drowsy London afternoon heavy with the scent of roses and lilac. Lord Henry Wotton — Harry to his friends — lies on a divan, smoking, watching his friend work on a portrait of extraordinary beauty: the full-length portrait of a young man of marvellous personal charm, Dorian Gray. Basil confesses that he will not exhibit it. He has put too much of himself into it, he says. There are secrets of his own soul in the canvas.

Lord Henry, with his lazy, musical voice, draws the confession out of him. Basil admits that he met Dorian at a party — saw a face so beautiful that it terrified him — and that the boy has become the entire motive of his art. Every day he has painted him: as Paris in armour, as Adonis with a leopard-skin, as a young Roman martyr. "He is all my art to me now," Basil says, in the most nakedly romantic passage Wilde ever wrote about friendship between men — and it is this passage, above all others, that would later be read aloud in a courtroom to destroy him.

Dorian's own history is sketched briefly and romantically: he is an orphan, the son of a beautiful mother who died young and a father killed in a duel, raised by a cold and wealthy grandfather, Lord Kelso, who never loved him. He has inherited a fortune and a face, and very little else — no profession, no duties, no experience of the world. He is, in Lord Henry's phrase, a blank page: and blank pages invite other people to write on them.

Basil is afraid of Lord Henry's influence. He begs him not to try to influence Dorian. Lord Henry answers with the amused, world-weary philosophy that will become the engine of the whole novel: influence is itself immoral, he says, because to influence a person is to give him one's own soul. But the warning comes too late. The door opens, and Dorian Gray himself walks into the studio, fresh from the garden, and Lord Henry meets him for the first time.

Dorian is twenty, and Wilde describes him as if describing a work of art: finely curved scarlet lips, frank blue eyes, crisp gold hair, a face of ivory and rose-leaf. He is shy, charming, unconscious of his own beauty. Basil presents his friend, and Lord Henry, delighted, begins at once to talk — to pour out the philosophy of pleasure and youth that he has been refining for years in London drawing-rooms, testing it now on a listener young enough to believe it.

They walk together in the garden while Basil finishes the portrait, and Lord Henry speaks to Dorian of youth as the one thing worth having in the world. Youth will not last, he tells him: the gold hair will turn grey, the red lips will lose their colour, the beauty will fade like a flower. And then what will be left? A life of dull routine, of respectable mediocrity. The only wisdom is to live the wonderful life that is in you, to seek out new sensations, to be afraid of nothing.

Basil's reluctance to exhibit the portrait has another, deeper motive, which he confesses only under pressure: he fears that if the world sees how much love went into the painting, it will guess the secret of his feeling for Dorian. In Victorian London, such devotion between men could not be named, and Basil — honest, awkward, deeply feeling — would rather hide his masterpiece than expose his heart. The portrait is already a kind of confession, and the world is not a safe confessor.

Dorian listens, and something in him changes as he listens. For the first time in his life he becomes conscious of his own beauty, and with that consciousness comes a stab of pain: the knowledge that it will pass. He has been a boy; in the course of one afternoon's conversation he begins to become something else — a young man awakened to himself, trembling on the edge of a philosophy that will devour him. Basil, watching from his easel, sees the change and is afraid.

When the portrait is finished, all three stand before it. It is Basil's masterpiece — Dorian Gray as he is at twenty, in all the splendour of his youth, painted with a love that makes the canvas seem alive. Dorian looks from the painting to himself in the mirror beside it, and the contrast strikes him like a physical blow. The portrait will stay young forever. He will grow old. And in that moment of anguish, half in jest and wholly in earnest, he makes the wish that seals his fate: that the picture might age instead of him, that he might stay always young while the canvas bears the burden of the years.

He does not know that wishes made before a work of art can come true. He only knows that he is suddenly jealous of his own painted image, and that Lord Henry's words are ringing in his ears like music. When Basil asks to keep the portrait for himself, Dorian refuses with a petulance that surprises them all. The painting will be his. It will hang where he can see it every day — a daily reminder of the youth he intends never to lose, and a daily temptation to the bargain he has already, in his heart, accepted.

chapters.title: Lord Henry's Gospel
paragraphs: Lord Henry Wotton is the serpent of this Eden, and Wilde gives him the best lines in the book — which is to say, some of the best lines in English literature. He is a brilliant, idle aristocrat who treats life as an experiment and other people as the subjects. His creed is simple: the aim of life is self-development, the realization of one's own nature, and the only way to do it is to yield to every impulse, to seek every sensation, to be afraid of nothing except dullness.

His most famous maxim is also his most dangerous: "The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it." He delivers it lightly, as a paradox for the dinner table, but Dorian receives it as a revelation. To the older man it is a witticism; to the boy it becomes a rule of life. That is the tragedy of Lord Henry: he plays with ideas as a child plays with matches, and never notices when the house catches fire.

He teaches Dorian that youth is the only wealth, beauty the only power. "To live is the rarest thing in the world," he tells him. "Most people exist, that is all." Existence — the dull round of work, duty, marriage, respectability — is a kind of death. Life is intensity, sensation, experience. He urges Dorian to treat his own personality as a work of art, to carve and polish it as a sculptor carves marble, and to let no moral convention stand in the way of its perfection.

He gives this philosophy a grand name: the New Hedonism. It is to be, he says, a more intelligent version of the old Greek pursuit of pleasure — not coarse indulgence but the refined, deliberate cultivation of experience, guided by the spirit of beauty. Dorian is to become its first perfect disciple: a young man who treats his life as a work of art and his soul as raw material. Lord Henry does not notice — or does not care — that he is describing a program for the systematic destruction of a human being.

There is a cold contempt in Lord Henry's philosophy for everything ordinary people value. He declares that nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing — a line that has outlived the novel and become a proverb. He mocks marriage, philanthropy, patriotism, and religion with equal elegance. He does not believe in sin, only in ugliness; he does not believe in virtue, only in charm. And Dorian, who has never heard anyone speak like this before, drinks it all in like a thirsty plant drinks rain.

Basil sees what is happening and is powerless to stop it. He watches his beautiful friend grow restless, discontented, hungry for experiences he cannot name. Lord Henry takes Dorian everywhere: to luncheons, to the opera, to dinners where the talk is all of art and scandal. He lends Dorian books, introduces him to curious people, fills his head with images of a life lived entirely for sensation. The painter's influence — the influence of love and admiration — is quietly displaced by the influence of ideas.

At lunch at his aunt Lady Agatha's, Lord Henry shows off his new discovery, and Dorian charms everyone at the table with his beauty and his shyness. It is Dorian's first appearance in society as Lord Henry's protege, and it is a triumph. Basil, watching, feels the boy slipping away from him with every witty remark Lord Henry makes. That evening, walking home alone, Basil understands that he has lost the most important struggle of his life — and that he lost it in a single afternoon, to a man who was only amusing himself.

What makes Lord Henry so seductive, and so destructive, is that he never acts on his own philosophy. He preaches the gospel of sensation while living a life of perfect, ironic detachment. He will not risk his own comfort for any experience; he experiments on Dorian instead. Wilde understood this type perfectly: the brilliant talker who treats other souls as raw material for his theories, and who walks away unscarred when the experiment ends in ruin.

Dorian, meanwhile, is transformed. The shy boy of the studio becomes a young man of fashion, confident, curious, and increasingly cold. He begins to look at the world the way Lord Henry looks at it: as a spectacle arranged for his amusement, as a series of sensations to be collected. When he falls in love, a few weeks later, he will fall in love in exactly this way — not with a woman, but with an image, an illusion, a performance. The seed Lord Henry planted in the garden is already flowering.

And the portrait hangs in Dorian's rooms, unchanged, beautiful, serene — a silent witness to the education of its original. It does not yet show any alteration. But the bargain has been struck, though neither Dorian nor the reader fully understands it yet. The picture will keep a record that Dorian himself refuses to keep: the record of what Lord Henry's gospel does to a soul, written not in words but in paint, line by line, year by year.

chapters.title: Sibyl Vane: The Actress
paragraphs: One evening Dorian comes to Lord Henry in a state of wild excitement: he is in love. He has discovered, in a shabby little theatre in a poor quarter of London, an actress of genius — a girl of seventeen named Sibyl Vane, who plays Shakespeare's heroines with a beauty and passion that have enchanted him utterly. He has gone night after night to watch her be Juliet, Rosalind, Imogen, Portia. He describes her as a marvel, a revelation, a creature from another world.

Lord Henry is amused and Basil is alarmed, but Dorian insists they come and see her. He paints a rapturous picture of her art: when she played Juliet, he tells them, the ugly theatre disappeared, the vulgar audience disappeared, and there was only the poetry, the love, the tragedy — made flesh in this slender girl with her great dark eyes. He is not in love with a person, though he does not know it yet. He is in love with art itself, with the illusion she creates.

The theatre itself is a place of faded, shabby magic: gilded cupids peeling on the ceiling, an audience of working people and rowdy youths, a manager who doubles as the tragedian. It is the last place one would expect to find genius — which is precisely why Dorian, with his new philosophy of seeking the extraordinary, is enchanted by it. He has stumbled on a pearl in a dunghill, and the contrast between the squalor of the place and the splendour of Sibyl's acting intoxicates him.

Sibyl Vane's own story is as touching as any of her roles. She lives with her mother, a faded actress, in shabby lodgings. Her brother James, a rough, devoted boy of sixteen, is about to sail for Australia to seek his fortune, and he makes his mother promise to watch over Sibyl. There is a mystery in the family: Sibyl and James have never known their father, and their mother speaks of him evasively, as a gentleman of high rank who loved her and could not marry her. James suspects the worst and swears that if any gentleman wrongs his sister, he will kill him.

For Sibyl, Dorian is "Prince Charming" — she does not even know his real name. He has come to her backstage, worshipped her, covered her with flowers, and spoken to her of love in language as romantic as the plays she acts in. To a girl who has lived her whole life inside Shakespeare's poetry, this beautiful young gentleman seems like a hero stepped out of one of her own plays. She tells her mother that she is loved, truly loved, and that nothing else in the world matters.

Wilde draws the contrast with delicate irony: Dorian loves Sibyl because she is an artist, because she gives him beautiful sensations; Sibyl loves Dorian because he seems to her the living embodiment of the romantic ideals she has acted on stage. Each loves an illusion. Neither loves the real, flawed, ordinary human being behind the illusion. It is a love built on artifice — and artifice, as the novel will show, is a fragile foundation for anything real.

Dorian's courtship is as theatrical as everything else about him. He proposes to Sibyl without knowing her surname, without having met her family, without a thought for the practical world — he proposes to Juliet, to Rosalind, to the idea of her. Sibyl accepts with the same unworldly rapture: she will leave the stage, she says, for she has found something better than acting. Neither of them understands that what each loves in the other is about to be destroyed by the very love they celebrate.

Dorian arranges for Lord Henry and Basil to attend Sibyl's performance as Juliet. He is radiant with pride and anticipation, certain that his friends will witness a triumph. He has told Sibyl nothing of his grand friends; he wants the evening to be a surprise, a coronation. As they take their seats in the shabby theatre, Dorian whispers that they are about to see the greatest actress of the age. He does not know that he is about to witness the destruction of everything he claims to love.

The scene is set for the novel's first great catastrophe. Up to now Dorian's corruption has been theoretical — ideas, conversations, attitudes. Now it will become real, in the most intimate and terrible way: in his treatment of another human being. The portrait in his rooms is still beautiful. But by the end of this night, it will have begun to change, and Dorian Gray will have taken the first step on the road that leads, eighteen years later, to murder.

chapters.title: The Night the Portrait Changed
paragraphs: The performance is a disaster. From her first entrance, Sibyl Vane acts badly — woodenly, falsely, without a spark of the genius Dorian has worshipped. Her voice is wrong, her gestures are stagey, her great love scenes fall flat. The audience grows restless; Lord Henry watches with ironic amusement; Basil with pity. And Dorian sits in gathering horror as the idol of his imagination crumbles before his eyes, night after night of enchantment exposed as a fraud.

He cannot understand it. This is the girl who was Juliet, who made poetry live. What has happened to her? After the play he goes backstage, wild with disappointment and anger, and demands an explanation. And Sibyl, radiant with happiness, gives him the answer — the most innocent and most fatal answer she could give. She tells him that she acted badly because she is in love, and love has made art unreal to her.

She explains it with the simplicity of a child: before she knew love, the stage was her reality — she lived in Shakespeare's world because she knew no other. But now she has known real love, real passion, and beside it the painted scenes and hollow verse seem empty. She does not need to act love anymore, because she feels it. She offers Dorian the truth of her heart, believing it is the greatest gift she can give him.

But Dorian does not want truth. He wanted the illusion. He tells her, with a cruelty that shocks even himself, that he loved her only for her art — that she has killed his love by killing the genius that inspired it. Without her acting she is nothing to him: shallow, ordinary, stupid. He throws her love back in her face and walks out, leaving her sobbing on the floor of her dressing-room, her "Prince Charming" revealed as a monster of selfishness.

Lord Henry, waiting outside, is philosophical about the whole affair. Women inspire us with the desire to do masterpieces, he remarks, and always prevent us from carrying them out. Dorian goes home alone, shaken but already beginning to justify himself: she had disappointed him, she had been unworthy of his love, he had acted rightly. He tells himself that a beautiful nature like his cannot be bound to mediocrity.

That night Dorian cannot sleep. He walks his rooms, he looks in mirrors, he tries to read — and always his mind returns to Sibyl's sobbing face and to the horrible ease with which the cruel words came to him. He had not known he could be cruel; Lord Henry's philosophy had taught him to admire selfishness as honesty, but it had not prepared him for the sight of real suffering caused by his own hand. For the first time, the gospel of sensation tastes like ashes.

The next morning brings the news: Sibyl Vane is dead. She took poison in the night — alone, in her shabby room, with no one to comfort her but the memory of a love that had turned to contempt. Dorian reads the announcement in the newspaper and is stunned. He had been angry; he had not imagined this. For a moment, genuine remorse touches him. He had a hand in a young girl's death, and the knowledge is terrible.

Then he looks at the portrait — and receives the second great shock of his life. Around the mouth of the painted Dorian Gray there is a new line, a touch of cruelty that was not there before, a sneer that the real Dorian's face does not show. The picture has changed. The wish he made in Basil's studio, half in jest, has come true: the canvas is bearing the record of his soul, registering the cruelty of last night while his own face remains untouched, beautiful, innocent.

At first he is terrified. Then, with Lord Henry's philosophy working in him like a slow poison, he begins to see the advantage. If the portrait will age and change instead of him — if it will carry the marks of every sin while he stays young and lovely — then he is free. Free to live as he pleases, to seek every sensation, to do as he wills, with no visible consequence. The picture will be his conscience, his diary, his secret judge — and no one else will ever know.

Lord Henry's consolation is a masterpiece of heartlessness disguised as wisdom. He tells Dorian that Sibyl has lived her finest tragedy — that her death was more beautiful than her life could ever have been, that she has passed into the realm of art where nothing can touch her. He speaks of her as one speaks of a character in a play, and gradually Dorian, soothed by the music of the voice, begins to see it that way too. By midnight he is calm. By the next day he is almost happy. The first murder of his soul is complete — and it was committed with words, over wine, by a friend.

He writes Sibyl a letter — a passionate, remorseful letter, full of self-reproach — but it is too late; she is already dead, and the letter is never sent. Instead he resolves, with a solemnity that is almost religious, to be good: the portrait will watch him, and he will resist temptation. The resolution lasts a single day. Lord Henry arrives, talks brilliantly about art and life, persuades him that Sibyl's death was itself a kind of beautiful tragedy — her finest performance — and Dorian, comforted, goes with him to the opera that very evening.

chapters.title: The Wish and the Bargain
paragraphs: To understand what has happened to Dorian Gray, we must return to the wish itself — that anguished cry in Basil Hallward's studio when the finished portrait first showed him his own beauty. Looking from the canvas to his reflection, Dorian had been seized by a jealousy so intense it felt like a physical pain: the picture would remain young forever, while he would grow old, wrinkled, and hideous. In his despair he had breathed the prayer that the portrait might age in his place — that he might keep his youth while the painting bore the burden of time and sin.

Wilde never explains the mechanism. There is no devil with a contract, no Mephistopheles, no explicit supernatural machinery — and that is part of the horror. The magic simply is, as inexplicable and as absolute as a fairy tale's. It may be a fantasy; it may be a metaphor made flesh. What matters is its moral meaning: Dorian has separated his soul from his body, his conscience from his face. He will live; the portrait will record the cost of his living.

The cruelty to Sibyl Vane was the first entry in that terrible diary. Dorian understands now, with a clarity that frightens him, that every evil thought, every cruel act, every surrender to base appetite will be written on the canvas while his own features stay smooth and blooming. He will be able to watch his own corruption as a spectator watches a play — with curiosity, even with a kind of scientific interest — without ever having to wear it.

There is a mirror in the story that Wilde returns to again and again: Dorian comparing his living face with the painted one, searching for differences, measuring his corruption. The portrait is the only mirror that tells him the truth. Ordinary mirrors flatter him — they show the unchanging beauty the world sees. Only the canvas shows what he is becoming. It is the most terrible gift ever given to a man: the gift of seeing his own soul, and being unable to bear the sight.

For a brief moment, this knowledge terrifies him into virtue. He tells himself that the portrait will be a constant warning, a visible conscience that will keep him from evil. He will resist Lord Henry's philosophy; he will live purely; he will make the picture a record of a noble life instead of a base one. It is a sincere resolution — and it shows that Dorian is not yet lost, that the better part of him still struggles against the worse.

But Lord Henry is always there, with his music and his paradoxes, to talk the better part down. He convinces Dorian that remorse is unhealthy, that the past is unchangeable, that Sibyl's death was picturesque — the romantic end of a romantic girl, far better than a long, dull life of mediocrity. Under this soothing philosophy, Dorian's resolve melts like snow. He decides to regard the whole affair as an artistic experience, a beautiful sorrow, a chapter in the development of his soul.

He even dreams, at first, of keeping a journal of the portrait's changes — of studying his own decay with the detachment of a scientist. The idea fascinates him: to watch sin write itself across a face, day by day, like an experiment in moral chemistry. It is Lord Henry's influence again — the transformation of horror into curiosity, of guilt into aesthetics. Dorian never writes the journal. He does not need to. The portrait writes itself, and he cannot stop reading it.

From this point the bargain takes full effect. Dorian locks the portrait away where no one can see it — first in a spare room, later in the disused schoolroom at the top of the house, covered with a heavy cloth, the door kept locked, the key always in his pocket. He visits it alone, in secret, watching with a horrible fascination as the slow changes accumulate: the mouth growing more sensual, the eyes more cunning, the whole face taking on an expression of corruption that his own living face never shows.

The double life begins. In society, Dorian Gray remains the most charming, the most beautiful, the most sought-after young man in London — ageing not at all as the years pass, a marvel that people remark upon with envy. In secret, he is becoming something else: a student of every forbidden pleasure, a collector of sensations, a man whose soul is being painted, stroke by stroke, in the locked room upstairs. The wish has given him everything he asked for. It will take, in return, everything he is.

chapters.title: The Yellow Book and the Years of Corruption
paragraphs: Soon after Sibyl Vane's death, Lord Henry sends Dorian a book — a strange, poisonous French novel, bound in yellow, that will shape the next eighteen years of his life. Wilde does not name it in the text, but every contemporary reader recognized it: it is Joris-Karl Huysmans's Against Nature, the bible of the Decadent movement, the story of a young Parisian aristocrat who withdraws from the world to cultivate every sensation in artificial perfection. Dorian reads it as a revelation, as a map of the life he is meant to lead.

The book's hero devotes himself to the senses with the seriousness of a scholar: he perfumes his rooms with rare essences, studies precious stones for their colours and their legends, collects embroidered vestments and exotic musical instruments. Dorian follows the same path, and Wilde devotes one of the novel's most famous chapters — the eleventh — to cataloguing his pursuits: perfumes from every corner of the earth, jewels with their strange histories and stranger superstitions, tapestries and textiles from vanished empires, music from every age.

The eleventh chapter — the catalogue of Dorian's pursuits — is the most purely beautiful and the most deliberately excessive passage in the novel. Wilde lavishes his learning on it: the Latin treatises on perfumes, the strange lore of jewels (the chrysolite that cures melancholy, the ruby that warns of poison), the ecclesiastical vestments heavy with gold thread, the musical instruments of vanished cultures. Critics have called it padding; admirers call it the point. It shows a man trying to fill the void where his soul was with beautiful things — and failing, magnificently.

This is not mere dilettantism. It is a philosophy: the life of the senses, pursued deliberately and refined to an art, as an alternative to the life of the soul. Dorian studies the influence of scents on the mind, the symbolism of gems, the lost crafts of dead civilizations. He becomes a connoisseur of everything beautiful and rare. And behind the connoisseurship, hidden from the world, runs a darker current: rumours of wilder pleasures, of nights in the lowest quarters of London, of appetites that the daylight world must never know.

The years pass — eighteen of them, in a single great sweep of narration — and Dorian does not age. At thirty-eight he looks twenty. People marvel; some whisper about a secret, about drugs or sorcery or a pact with the devil. His reputation, meanwhile, darkens steadily. Young men who become his intimate friends come to grief: one ruins himself, another flees the country, a third takes his own life. Fathers forbid their sons to know him; decent women grow cold when he enters a room; invitations become fewer, and those that come are edged with unease.

At a dinner at Lady Narborough's, years later, Dorian overhears the talk circling around him like sharks: the ruined boy who shot himself in a gambling den, the young guardsman found dead with a smile on his face, the artist who fled to America. No one accuses him directly — his charm forbids it — but the stories attach themselves to his name like burrs. He smiles, he talks brilliantly, he is the life of the table. And all the while he is thinking of the locked room upstairs, and wondering how much longer beauty can protect him.

Yet no one can prove anything, and his beauty remains his shield. How can this gracious, charming, unfading youth be guilty of the things whispered about him? The world, which judges by surfaces — as Lord Henry taught it to do — cannot reconcile the lovely face with the ugly rumours, and so the rumours remain rumours. Only the locked room upstairs knows the truth, and Dorian visits it less and less often now, for each visit shows him a face more hideous than the last.

Wilde returns obsessively to the theme of poisonous books — books that corrupt the reader who loves them. Lord Henry says that the books the world calls immoral are simply books that show the world its own shame; but the yellow book really does poison Dorian, or rather, it gives his corruption a shape and a philosophy. It teaches him to systematize what Lord Henry only sketched: to make a religion of sensation, with rituals, vestments, and sacred texts. Dorian becomes the book's most faithful reader — and its final victim.

Wilde is careful never to specify Dorian's worst sins. The novel hints, suggests, and falls silent — and the silence is more terrible than any catalogue could be. We are told of opium dens, of secret vices, of a life lived entirely for sensation without regard for any other human being. The vagueness is deliberate: each reader fills the blank with their own imagination, and the portrait in the attic becomes a mirror for whatever corruption the reader most fears.

What is certain is the spiritual result. Dorian has become exactly what Lord Henry's philosophy promised: a man who has developed every capacity for pleasure and atrophied every capacity for love, pity, and remorse. He is courteous, generous with money, delightful in company — and utterly hollow. He has treated his own soul as Lord Henry treated ideas: as material for experiment. And the experiment's result hangs upstairs under its cloth, growing more loathsome with every passing year.

Only two people from the old days still have any claim on him: Basil Hallward, who loves him still and watches his decline with breaking heart, and Lord Henry, who finds his creation endlessly amusing and never asks what the amusement costs. The stage is set for the novel's second great catastrophe — the night Basil comes to confront his lost friend, and learns the secret of the locked room.

chapters.title: Basil Confronts Dorian
paragraphs: It is the night before Basil Hallward is to leave for Paris, where he will work undisturbed for six months. He has heard the rumours about Dorian for years and has refused to believe them; but now, on the eve of his departure, he can bear the silence no longer. He comes to Dorian's house late at night, unannounced, and begs for the truth. He speaks of the young men ruined, the lives wrecked, the doors closed. He asks Dorian, as a friend who has loved him since boyhood, to deny it all.

Basil has been writing to Dorian for months, and Dorian has not answered. The painter's last letter — unsent, found later among his papers — is full of bewildered affection: he cannot reconcile the beautiful boy he loved with the rumours he hears, and he begs for one honest conversation. It is this unanswered letter that drives him to the house that night. He will have his conversation. He does not know it will be his last.

Dorian listens with cold amusement. He is no longer the boy Basil painted; he is a man of thirty-eight with the face of twenty, and his patience with moral lectures is exhausted. When Basil presses him — when he speaks of the soul, of prayer, of repentance — something snaps in Dorian. He decides, in a flash of terrible impulse, to show Basil the truth: to let the painter see what his masterpiece has become, and what its original has become with it.

He takes a lamp and leads Basil up the stairs to the disused schoolroom, unlocks the door, and tears the cloth from the portrait. What Basil sees freezes the blood. The face on the canvas is still recognizably Dorian Gray's — the same features, the same composition — but it is bloated, sensual, and cruel beyond belief: the eyes have the cunning of secret vice, the mouth is twisted with a hideous sneer, and the whole visage seems to exhale corruption like a miasma. It is the face of a soul eighteen years deep in sin.

The locked room is described with the precision of a nightmare: the schoolroom of Dorian's childhood, high under the eaves, long disused, its furniture shrouded in dust-sheets, the portrait hidden under a heavy purple-and-gold cloth that Dorian himself made to cover it. Basil looks around at this secret chapel of corruption — the place where, for eighteen years, his friend has come alone to worship the record of his own decay — and understands, too late, everything.

Basil stares in horror, and at first he cannot believe it is his own work — then he recognizes his brushwork, his signature, and understands. He falls back, aghast, and begs Dorian to pray, to repent, to ask forgiveness while there is still time. He speaks of mercy, of the possibility of redemption, of the God he still believes in. It is the last sincere moral voice Dorian will ever hear, and it speaks in the locked room at midnight, before the painted record of a ruined life.

Dorian's response is not repentance but rage. The sight of the portrait — his own soul made visible — fills him not with contrition but with hatred: hatred of Basil for having painted it, for having seen it, for existing as a witness to his secret. In that hatred, all the corruption of eighteen years concentrates into a single murderous instant. He seizes a knife from a chest — the same knife, as it will prove, with which his story will end — and stabs Basil Hallward again and again until the painter lies dead at the foot of his own ruined masterpiece.

The murder is the point of no return. Until now Dorian's sins, however dark, have been sins of indulgence; now he has taken a human life, the life of the one man who truly loved him. Wilde narrates the aftermath with cold, almost clinical precision: Dorian's first thought is not remorse but concealment. He calmly rings for his servant, invents a story, and sits down to think. By morning he has a plan — and the plan requires the help of an old friend.

That friend is Alan Campbell, once a brilliant young scientist, now a broken man whose career Dorian helped to destroy. Dorian summons him and, with a letter already written, blackmails him into disposing of the body: Campbell, a chemist, must dissolve it in nitric acid in the very room where it lies, leaving no trace. Campbell resists, begs, threatens — and finally yields, driven upstairs like a man walking to his own execution. By evening the thing is done. Basil Hallward has vanished from the world, and no one will ever know how.

Dorian feels, at first, a strange relief — even exhilaration. The witness is gone; the secret is safe. He goes to the opera that night and charms everyone as usual. But upstairs, under its cloth, the portrait has registered the murder, and when Dorian next looks at it he sees that the hands are red — red with blood that will not wash off. The diary of his soul has a new entry, written in the brightest and most terrible colour of all.

chapters.title: The Opium Den and James Vane
paragraphs: After the murder, Dorian flees London for the docks, to one of the squalid opium dens where he has long been a secret visitor. He goes to drown memory in drugged stupor — to forget the locked room, the red hands on the canvas, the chemist's ashen face. But the past is waiting for him there in human form. As he leaves the den, a woman in the doorway, seeing his beautiful young face, calls out mockingly that they should not sell him short: he is "Prince Charming," she says, the gentleman who drove poor Sibyl Vane to her death eighteen years ago.

A man standing in the shadows hears her. It is James Vane — Sibyl's brother, grown to a hard, weathered sailor, back in England after years in Australia. He has never forgotten his vow: the night before he sailed, he swore that if any man wronged his sister, he would find him and kill him. For eighteen years he has nursed that promise. Now, hearing the name "Prince Charming," he follows Dorian into the fog with a revolver in his pocket and murder in his heart.

The opium den is drawn from Wilde's knowledge of London's darkest corners: a narrow room with bunk beds, the sweet heavy smoke, the lost faces of men and women seeking forgetfulness. Dorian is known here, and not as a gentleman — here he is just another customer of oblivion. The contrast between this squalor and the brilliant drawing-rooms where he spends his evenings measures the full distance of his fall.

He catches Dorian in a dark archway and presses the gun to his head. Dorian, with the quick cunning of terror, begs for a light to see his attacker's face — and when the match flares, James sees what appears to be a boy of twenty, far too young to have been Sibyl's lover eighteen years before. He hesitates. The woman from the den runs up, furious at losing her amusement, and tells him the truth: the gentleman has not aged a day in eighteen years; it is some devil's bargain, but he is the man. James realizes his mistake too late — Dorian has vanished into the fog.

From that night, Dorian is a haunted man. He knows James Vane is hunting him, and for the first time in years he feels real fear — not the abstract fear of discovery, but the physical fear of a bullet. He flees to the country, to the house of friends, hoping to hide among shooting parties and dull company. But James has followed him. For days Dorian glimpses a sailor's face watching him from the woods, from the road, from the edge of the crowd — always watching, always waiting.

The end comes with terrible irony during a shooting party. A hare is started in the bracken; the guns fire; and one of the beaters cries out that a man has been hit. They carry the body in — a sailor, shot through the chest, dead. Dorian goes to look, sick with a hope he dares not name, and sees the face of James Vane. The hunter is dead by misadventure, killed by a stray shot meant for game. Dorian is safe.

At the inquest, the death is ruled an accident — a beater shot in mistake for a hare — and the world moves on. No one connects the dead sailor with Dorian Gray; no one knows that James Vane even existed. Dorian attends the funeral in secret and feels, obscurely, that a debt has been paid. But debts in this novel are never paid: they are only transferred, from the living to the dead, from the soul to the canvas, accumulating interest in the dark.

He should feel relief, and at first he does — a wild, almost hysterical relief. But as he stands over the body, something else stirs in him: the recognition that this dead man is the brother of the girl he destroyed, that his own sins have now claimed a second life from the same innocent family. He has not pulled the trigger, but the chain of causation runs straight from his cruelty in Sibyl's dressing-room to this corpse on the grass. The portrait upstairs, could he see it now, would have grown a shade more hideous.

Back in London, Dorian tries to resume his life, but the fear has changed him. He is nervous, restless, unable to sleep. He tells Lord Henry that he is going to reform, to be good — and Lord Henry laughs, as he always laughs, and talks him out of it with a paradox. But the seed of the idea has been planted, not by philosophy but by terror. For the first time, Dorian Gray genuinely wants to escape himself — and the only escape he can imagine is one final, desperate act of goodness.

chapters.title: A Single Good Deed
paragraphs: In the country, before the shooting party, Dorian had met a village girl named Hetty Merevale — pretty, innocent, romantic, the daughter of decent poor people. In the old days he would have amused himself with her and abandoned her, as he has amused himself with so many. This time, moved by his new resolve, he does the opposite: he leaves her alone. He does not write, does not pursue, does not compromise her. He spares her — deliberately, consciously — and he is proud of it. It is, he tells himself, the first good action of his life.

He hurries back to London full of hope and tells Lord Henry what he has done, expecting admiration. Lord Henry is amused and unconvinced: he suggests that Hetty is probably crying her heart out, and that Dorian's "goodness" has been crueller than seduction would have been. But Dorian will not be talked out of his triumph this time. He goes upstairs to the locked room, draws back the cloth, and looks at the portrait — expecting, longing, to see some sign of improvement, some softening of that hideous face.

Dorian's resolve to be good takes a strange form: he does not confess, does not make restitution, does not seek out those he has harmed. He simply decides, as one decides on a new hobby, to perform a good action and watch the portrait improve. Even his repentance is aesthetic — an experiment, a test of the magic. He wants to see virtue work the way vice worked: visibly, dramatically, on canvas. The portrait, which records motives and not gestures, is unimpressed.

What he sees strikes him like a blow. The portrait has changed — but not for the better. The face is, if anything, more loathsome than before: and now, added to the cruelty and sensuality, there is a new expression, sly and self-satisfied — the unmistakable look of the hypocrite. His "good deed" has been registered on the canvas not as virtue but as vanity: he spared Hetty not for her sake but for his own, to admire himself in the mirror of his own magnanimity.

It is the most devastating moment in the novel. Dorian understands, at last, that he cannot cheat the portrait. The canvas does not record actions; it records motives. Every attempt to use goodness as a means — to buy back his soul with a single calculated act of mercy — only adds a new layer of corruption: the corruption of self-deception. He is not merely wicked; he is wicked and self-righteous about it, which is worse.

He confesses everything to Lord Henry — or nearly everything — in their last great conversation, walking in the garden as they walked eighteen years before. He speaks of the portrait (without revealing its secret), of his weariness, of his desire to be good. Lord Henry, faithful to the end, treats it all as a pose, a new sensation, the latest interesting development in his favourite experiment. He cannot conceive that Dorian is serious, because he has never been serious about anything in his life.

He stands before the picture in despair. Eighteen years of pleasures have left him empty; one attempted virtue has left him exposed. There is no way forward and no way back. He cannot undo the bargain — the wish cannot be unwished. He cannot live with the portrait — each sight of it is a torment. And he cannot destroy his conscience without destroying the only witness to what he has become. Or can he? A terrible new thought begins to form in his mind.

The portrait is the evidence. It is the diary, the accuser, the thing that knows. If it were destroyed — slashed, burned, annihilated — would the past be destroyed with it? Would the bargain be broken? Dorian begins to imagine the canvas in ruins, the painted soul obliterated, himself left alone with his youth and his beauty and no witness to accuse him. It is the logic of a desperate man, the last fantasy of a soul that has exhausted every other escape.

He takes down the knife — the knife with which he killed Basil Hallward, which he has kept all these years — and stands before the portrait in the locked room at midnight. He looks at the hideous face that is truly his, and at his own young face in the mirror beside it, and he makes his choice. He will kill the past. He will stab the thing that has tormented him, and be free at last. He raises the knife and drives it into the canvas.

chapters.title: The Knife and the Portrait
paragraphs: The servants hear it first: a cry, terrible in its agony, ringing through the silent house at midnight — a cry such as they have never heard from human lips. Then silence. They wake, they whisper, they are afraid to go upstairs. At last, two of them creep up to the locked schoolroom door and find it — to their astonishment — unlocked from the inside. They push it open and go in.

On the wall hangs the portrait of Dorian Gray, in all the wonder of his exquisite youth and beauty — splendid, serene, untouched, exactly as Basil Hallward painted it on that summer day in the studio eighteen years before. Not a line of cruelty mars the mouth; not a shadow of corruption clouds the eyes. It is the masterpiece restored, the young god reborn, lovelier than ever for the darkness through which it has passed.

And on the floor beneath it lies a dead man, in evening dress, with a knife in his heart. He is withered, wrinkled, and loathsome of visage — an old man worn down by every vice the flesh is heir to, his face a mask of horror and decay. The servants do not know him. It is only when they look closer, at the rings glittering on his swollen fingers, that they recognize their master.

The cry the servants hear is described as horrible in its agony — the sound, one imagines, of a soul being torn from a body, or of eighteen years of corruption finding a voice at last. It is the only moment in the novel when Dorian's suffering becomes audible, when the beautiful mask drops and the truth screams. Then silence: the silence of a house in which the master will never speak again.

Dorian Gray has killed himself. In stabbing the portrait — in trying to murder his own soul, the witness and record of his corruption — he has turned the knife on the only part of him that was still truly alive. The bargain is broken at last, and broken in the only way it could be broken: the magic reverses itself in the instant of its destruction. The painting is restored to its original beauty; the man takes on, in death, the hideousness the painting bore for him in life.

The portrait's restoration is the novel's final paradox, and its final mercy. The painting — Basil's love made visible — is cleansed; the man — Dorian's choices made flesh — is condemned. Art survives the artist's corruption; beauty outlives the beast who wore it. Wilde, who believed that art was independent of the artist's morals, could hardly have devised a more perfect emblem of his creed: the work remains pure, even when the life that inspired it has rotted away.

Wilde's ending is as perfect, in its way, as a Greek tragedy. Every element of the story converges in that locked room: the wish made in the studio, the philosophy preached in the garden, the cruelty to Sibyl, the eighteen years of secret sin, the murder of Basil with this same knife. Dorian's last act is characteristic to the end — an attempt to escape consequence by destroying the evidence — and it brings the one consequence he never imagined: the evidence survives, and he does not.

There is a final, terrible irony in the servants' recognition. They know their master only by his rings — by the ornaments of wealth, the surface things. The face means nothing to them. It is Wilde's last comment on a world that judges by appearances: the beautiful portrait on the wall is a lie, the hideous corpse on the floor is the truth, and no one who knew Dorian Gray in life would ever have guessed which was which.

And so the bargain ends where it began: before a portrait, in a silent room, with beauty looking down on ruin. Dorian Gray wanted to live forever without paying for his life. The canvas kept the accounts, and at midnight the debt came due.

chapters.title: Legacy: Beauty, Influence, and the Moral
paragraphs: Wilde always denied that his novel preached a moral, and the Preface says so plainly: "There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written, or badly written. That is all." Yet readers have never been able to take him at his word, because the story itself seems to demonstrate, with the force of a fable, that a life devoted to beauty without goodness ends in horror. Dorian gets everything he wished for — eternal youth, endless pleasure, freedom from consequence — and it destroys him. If that is not a moral, it is a very convincing imitation of one.

Perhaps the paradox is the point. Wilde believed that art should not moralize, but he could not prevent his art from meaning. The Picture of Dorian Gray is, among other things, a Faust story for the modern age: like Goethe's scholar, Dorian trades his soul for what he most desires, and like all such bargains in literature, this one comes due. The portrait is his Mephistopheles and his conscience in one — the supernatural made psychological, the old legend rewritten as a study of what happens inside a human mind.

The book's afterlife in popular culture has been extraordinary: dozens of films, plays, operas, and ballets; Dorian Gray as a character in other writers' novels; the very name turned into an adjective — "Dorian Gray" for anyone who seems not to age, "a portrait in the attic" for any hidden corruption. Few novels have so completely escaped their covers and entered the language. Wilde would have been delighted: he always said he wanted to be a legend, and legends are what people quote without reading.

The novel's influence has been immense. It became the defining book of the Decadent movement, the gospel of art for art's sake, and the scandal that helped destroy its author. After Wilde's trial and imprisonment, the book was read for decades as a coded confession, a glimpse into forbidden London. Later generations discovered in it something else: a pioneering work of psychological horror, a study of narcissism and influence, a fable about the image-obsessed culture that Wilde, with uncanny foresight, seemed to predict.

Lord Henry's epigrams escaped the novel and entered the language. "The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it." "Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing." "To live is the rarest thing in the world. Most people exist, that is all." People quote them who have never read the book — often without realizing that in the novel, these glittering lines are the instruments of a young man's destruction. Wilde's wit was so bright that it blinded readers to the darkness underneath.

There is a final sense in which Wilde was right to deny the moral. The novel does not preach; it shows. It does not say "do not do this" — it says "this is what doing it looks like," and leaves the reader to shudder. That is why the book survives every change of fashion: each generation finds its own portrait in the attic, its own bargain with youth, its own Lord Henry whispering that the only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it. The magic was never in the canvas. It was in us, all along.

That darkness is what keeps the novel alive. Beneath the comedy of manners and the perfumed prose, Dorian Gray is one of the most frightening books ever written: frightening because its monster is not a creature but a charming young man, because its horror is not supernatural but moral, because its question — what would you sacrifice to stay young and beautiful forever? — is one that every age, and perhaps ours most of all, must answer. The portrait hangs in our imagination still, changing, while we look away.

Wilde died in Paris in 1900, five years after his release from prison, broken in health and fortune but unbroken in wit. He never wrote another novel. The Picture of Dorian Gray remains his single, perfect contribution to the form: a book its author claimed was about nothing but beauty, which turned out to be about everything — youth and age, influence and responsibility, art and life, the soul and the price of selling it. All art is at once surface and symbol, he wrote. Beneath this exquisite surface, the symbol waits, patient as a portrait in a locked room, for each new reader to come and look.
